Kristina Norman is an artist and documentary filmmaker working in Tallinn, who can be considered the unrivalled most successful artist to have debuted in Estonia in the 2000s in the context of the international artworld. She is, to date, the youngest artist to have represented Estonia at the international Venice Art Biennale (2009), and as of 2011 her works belong to prestigious museum collections both in Estonia (Kumu Art Museum) and in Finland (Kiasma). 
The present work was created for the EV 100 anniversary exhibition held at the Tallinn Art Hall. The text accompanying the exhibition excellently describes this work that captivates with the charm of ethnic song: "Gods, give us back the fire" comments on the recent discussion about why it is not possible to sing a song in Russian

During the time spent and experienced in Thailand, Proosa's focus of interest has been Thailand's numerous transgender women – kathoeys. The desire to belong to a community is universal, and thus there is nothing unusual in the fact that Proosa, who likewise identifies as transgender, blossomed upon arriving in Thailand, finding both herself and love.
As an artist, Proosa is captivated above all by the portrait. Whether photographing others or herself, her gaze seems to move simultaneously on two axes: on the one hand unconditional admiration for the person portrayed, and on the other a longing to treat the camera as a mirror. 17abbfa770c0d5c471e32fc4a70f74970e5155b9: Raul Meel represents the radical wing of Estonian art renewal of the 1970s–1980s and is known as the most famous autodidact and outsider in Estonian art. Meel's desire to speak the same language as Western art renewal meant renouncing the customary possibilities and signifiers that had grown out of the Estonian art system itself. An artist with an engineering background, he began in 1970 a dialogue between art and exact science, which paved the way for the arrival of the conceptualist notion of art in Estonia and proved that visual art too is capable of reflecting the spiritually complex problems brought about by contemporary developments. Osvald Timmas (1913-2005) was one of the best-known Estonian exile artists and a member of the Royal Canadian Academy of Arts. Born on Saaremaa, the artist studied economics at the University of Tartu in 1937-1944 and devoted himself to art only after emigrating, in Canada, in the 1960s.
Timmas's main field was watercolour, in which he was highly innovative, depicting micro- and macrostructures, the underwater world, rocks, etc. He enriched watercolour technique by using iron rust.
In 1990 the Adamson-Eric Museum held a solo exhibition of Osvald Timmas. The Art Museum of Estonia holds 28 works in the print collection and 2 works in the painting collection. Two 1832 watercolours by A. W. G. Pezold ("Eva" and "Barrel Kaarel") donated to the Art Museum of Estonia from Germany are of great art-historical value. These are early depictions of Estonians created by the well-known Baltic German Estophile August Pezold (1794-1859). Although without surnames, these are certainly specific persons, from Tarvastu manor and Viljandi. Based on Pezold's 1832 watercolours, lithographs were made in G. F. Schlater's workshop in Tartu in 1834, and altered reprints in 1852, of which the Art Museum of Estonia's print collection holds "Eva from Põltsamaa" (EKM G 4517). The lithograph "Barrel Kaarel" is not held by EKM, but exists in the Estonian National Museum and the Tartu Art Museum.

The best-known print series by the outstanding artist and teacher Kaljo Põllu (1934-2010) are "The Kodalased" and "The Power of the Kalevs" (1970s).
In the 1980s the author continued in the same direction, but in a larger format with colour mezzotints, and this stage also includes "Heaven and Earth" from 1987 and "Eternal Greeting" from 1988. Põllu continued to engage with mythological, cosmogonic themes that had long inspired him.
These later prints form the series "Heaven and Earth". Natalie Mei's (1900-1975) small watercolour portrait of her fellow artist Karin Luts (1904-1993) dates from 1929.
A young woman in modern dress, with a short coat, patent-leather shoes and a reticule, is depicted, however, in a caricatured manner. Karin Luts's characteristic profile is emphasised in the woman's face, and the legs seem to be drawn as if with a ruler. Such an approach is explained by the artist's inscription on the picture: Artist Karin Luts. Natalie Mei, like Karin Luts, was in the 1920s a fighter for the rights of Estonian women artists and of women in general. For this purpose, an emphatically ladylike yet at the same time odd, caricaturing manner of depiction was well suited. Both the author and the person depicted are among the most important representatives of the first Estonian modernist women artists

The photo comes from Cloe Jancis and Sigrid Viir's exhibition "On some more energetic days you put on your mask too firmly in front of the mirror, so that it bites into your skin". The impulse for the birth of the exhibition was the project "Isolation Dialogues" initiated by the Photography Museum in spring 2020, the aim of which was to document the sense of the isolation period and the newly arisen situation. The title of the exhibition comes from a short essay by Maris Karjatse.
The artists' visual dialogue proceeded by interpreting, mixing and further developing each other's ideas. Their dialogue brings out humour and absurdity as one possible defence mechanism and way out of mental and physical hardship during the isolation period. The photographs are supported by installational frames.
35a4c2e5eabca7f99008a93b0f9384693064a48a: The unsigned engraving is small but very expressive, in a so-called rain-hatching and sketch-like, restless manner. This is apparently an expressionist work of art from the period after World War I. Since at that time (1923–1924) the print teacher at the Pallas Art School in Tartu was the well-known German modernist Magnus Zeller (1888–1972), the work is associated with his oeuvre. The artist took part in World War I as a soldier and witnessed the horrors of war directly. Zeller came to Estonia in 1918 with the German forces and became acquainted with Estonian artists (K. Mägi, A. Vabbe, A. Tassa). M. Zeller was a print teacher for three semesters at the Pallas Art School, founded in Tartu in 1919. He later lived in Berlin and in Caputh near Potsdam, and died in East Berlin in 1972.

6031e458145484228ff2db9dccb746d3551e2318: Mart Pert (Pärt) (1898-1993) was a set designer and drawing teacher, who studied from 1915 to 1921 at the State School of Applied Art, from which he was given, in 1938, a certificate of applied artist in the field of set painting. In the 1920s he founded a centre for the production of stage sets at the Estonian Education Union, where sets were made for nearly 200 productions. From 1935 he worked as the artistic director of the Estonian Home Embellishment Society, and from 1945 he worked as a teacher of drawing and handicraft at the Aruküla school. Pert's illustrations and graphic art from the early 20th century are interesting examples of the artistic creation of the era, which relate strongly to the oeuvre of Wiiralt and other artists of the time.
174ec09c9f0d32e0b4487d8c541447c84782b045:
One of the best-known stories about the censorship of Pikker dates from 1979, when issue 17 of the magazine published a caricature by Heiki Ernits dedicated to the Year of the Child, depicting the Ulyanov family. That the caricature was published is a sign that the censor did not notice the allusion to the Ulyanov family. The incident did not remain without consequences. The editor-in-chief of Pikker received a reprimand, Heiki Ernits was forced to interrupt his studies at the Moscow film courses, and he was threatened with a permanent publication ban.
Heiki Ernits graduated in 1975 from the Tallinn Pedagogical Institute in the speciality of art and craft education. In 1978 he went to work in the animation department of Tallinnfilm, where he has worked as an animation film artist and later as a director.
9e26f7c7212944304a6272a5a94bff5a61b1df85:
Wilhelm Siegfried Stavenhagen's (1814-1881) Album of Views of Livonia (1866) contains 40 steel engravings together with German-language texts.
Working as a land surveyor and cartographer, Stavenhagen is primarily known as the compiler of his three luxurious albums (Estland, Livland, Kurland), which were published in 1866-1867, with views of Narva also included. Numerous reprints of the engravings were made, including as lithographs.
This album has bound into it 40 views from various historical governorates (cf. ERM K 2329/1-90).
The Art Museum of Estonia's collection has to date an album of views of Estland with 30 sheets (G 22827), plus occasional various individual views. The steel engravings hold international significance in the history of 19th-century view graphics.

The photo comes from the exhibition "On some more energetic days you press your mask too firmly against your face in front of the mirror, so that it bites into your skin". The initial impulse for the exhibition's creation was the project "Isolation Dialogues" initiated by the Estonian Museum of Photography in spring 2020, the aim of which was to document the perception of the time of isolation and the newly arisen situation. The exhibition's title comes from a short essay by Maris Karjatse.
The artists' visual dialogue proceeded by interpreting, mixing and further developing each other's ideas. Their dialogue brings out humour and absurdity as one possible defence mechanism and a way out of mental and physical constraint during the time of isolation. The photographs are supported by installational frames.
81a1dd86e77007315d81dd3415449405856ae46d:
The album consists of a cover cut from two tin cans, 9 sheets, and metal hooks holding them together. On the outer side of the front cover there are five lines of text in variously designed script (in German, the words remain partly truncated). On the outer side of the back cover, upside down, long hanging pepper pods with stem and leaves. On both covers green and brown print on a yellow background. On the front cover, on the right, tilted, a red double sticker with black lettering.
On the first and last sheet, a collage of irregular shapes glued one on top of another, covered by a network of pencil and ballpoint pen lines. The edges of the shapes are black. On the other sheets square grey photographs of faces are glued on.
6646dc3b4859406735636b3d9bf195c9ae40b0bf: In the upper left quarter of the sheet: on the left a man carrying a sack on his back, sweat running down his face, on the sack the text WÕLAD; behind him, on the right, seen frontally, another man carrying a sack, on the sack the text WÕLAD. In the upper right quarter of the sheet: in the foreground the bust of a man in a bowler hat, behind him on the left Vanemuine sitting on a rock and weeping, beside him sits a naked child sucking its finger. In the lower left quarter of the sheet: in the foreground the half-figures of two men holding each other by the shoulders, behind them, on the left, the full figures of three men. In the lower right quarter of the sheet: on the left in front, the half-figure of a man bent half over, at whom bottles are being thrown at the head from a counter behind him.
011ea0f23f8761b57dffd3bda63cf2addbd2f6c9: Kaljo Põllu (1934-2010) was one of the most legendary figures of Estonian culture, in whose life's work an important place is held by the mythological print series "Kodalased" and "Kalivägi", created in the 1970s and 1980s. These works carried a national significance and, in their time, also a worldview-related weight. Today, thanks to their high artistic level, Kaljo Põllu's print series speak in a very unique way also to an international art audience. The works being accepted into the collection of the Art Museum of Estonia represent works by Põllu that have so far been absent from the collections of Estonian public museums. Some sheets are also unique single copies - early proof prints of the artist's idea sketches.
ea698053a218a199f3e1fb66f3b457a3ee75ee38: He studied art history in 1919-1921 and 1927-1931 at the University of Tartu and in 1931 at the University of Helsinki. He belonged to the South Estonian art protection committee in 1919. He was head of the art and caricature department of Postimees in 1920-1922, teacher of painting and analytical drawing at Pallas in 1925-1929, editor and co-author of the art department of the "Estonian Encyclopaedia" in 1932-1934, adviser to the State Propaganda Bureau in 1935-1940, and at the same time editor of the art department of the journal Varamu in 1938-1939. In 1941 he moved to Germany, lived in Freudenstadt, where he worked as an artist and art critic, contributing to the journals Tulimuld and Mana. He published several important monographs (E. Wiiralt, A. Vabbe)
d110d26063676b1712b6c8412563155d09edc5fa: Leonhard Lapini's pair of works "Jänku suudlus" ["The Rabbit's Kiss"] and "Kunstnik" ["The Artist"] (in addition to the 1970 lithographs, author's repetitions were also made in offset print in 1996) is a vivid example of so-called compound pop – a version of pop art practised in Soviet Estonia, whose method included the (self-)ironic interpretation of the surrounding Soviet everyday life and visual culture. Thus the artist used a representational system borrowed from children's colouring books to stage absurd situations, which are connected, among other things, with themes of art-making. This pair holds an iconic status in recent Estonian art history and belongs to the permanent Soviet-period exhibition of the Kumu Art Museum.
cc943259ace9b089f076dedfd9fe67cf5c160d54:
In the foreground a woman playing the piano on a chair with a high back, behind her on the left a child on a similar smaller chair, likewise turned half towards the right. In the back on the right a violinist in an S-shaped pose. Above on the right a window through which a crescent moon can be seen. On the piano a kerosene lamp. The players cast shadows on the walls.

On the verso: in the foreground 5 lying lions. From left to right: below a lion's head in profile facing right, eyes closed, above on the left a lion en face, head turned 1/4 to the left, above in the middle a lion en face, eyes open, and below a lion turned half to the right, jaws open. In the middle below a small branching cactus. Dark background. The right-hand part of the composition has been cut off.
c19dad339f4c3c43a83d08470e963af905d2fa43: Karl Pärsimägi (1902-1942) began his art studies as a schoolboy in Konrad Mägi's studio and continued at Pallas in 1919-1926 as a student of Konrad Mägi and Ado Vabbe, and from 1932 as a student of Vabbe, completing the school's practical course in 1936. The artist's further path led to Paris, where Pärsimägi improved himself in private academies and by copying works of old masters in museums. His body of work consists of oil and watercolour paintings and monotypes, characterised by a fauvist, intimate mood based on local colours. The 1935 work "Female Nude" also bears witness to the painterly language characteristic of Pärsimägi, marked by the use of pure colour surfaces.
560cfc597e79565dbed428abd7b30e75b6352600: A work with an interesting legend in Anton Starkopf's oeuvre. It is a portrait of the property master of Vanemuine theatre at that time. The model was made so that August Lomp, a joiner by training who had shown formal talent, would carve a wooden portrait of himself under Starkopf's guidance. The initial body, glued together from oak wood, was carved through to its finishing. The work took place at Vallikraavi 18, where the Vanemuise property workshop was located at the time. Unfortunately, in 1950 Starkopf went to Moscow and the work was left unfinished and was destroyed in the intervening period. August Lomp was sent to a Russian prison camp in Karelia, from which his grandmother later smuggled him out with the help of civilian clothing.
570d37cb7846323d5b7b81ad52e6d4b349f6efef: The work depicts the artists who participated in the semi-official art event "Sündmus Harku '75" ["Event Harku '75"], which took place in 1975 at the Harku manor (at the time the Institute of Experimental Biology) on the outskirts of Tallinn. The work, created after a photograph, depicts among others also its author I. Paul, whose participation in the event, which has become legendary, has on several occasions gone unmentioned. This work thus offers, on the one hand, an interesting example of the interpretation of a photograph in graphic art, and, on the other, has documentary value as a record of a landmark art event that has entered Estonian art history, complementing the accompanying materials (works, photographic records, etc.) held in the collection of the Art Museum of Estonia.
19e15967a0ce515c59f7fc73ba92e2c6386d7489:
The works of Otto Paju (1926-2016) are a valuable addition to the so-far fragmentary body of work by this expatriate Estonian artist in the collection of the Art Museum of Estonia.
Born in Rakvere, having studied art in Stockholm and Oslo and worked as a landscape architect, Paju was a book designer and also an active organiser of Estonian art life in Sweden.
His series consisting of eighteen relief prints is a good example of Paju's assimilation into Swedish art life. The sheets with abstracted forms are masterly both in form and colour. The same selection of works was also exhibited at Otto Paju's memorial exhibition at the Estonian House in Stockholm on 9-29 March 2017.
06e2659db94634170f701b483aa5cadc8b8209a0:
Ilmar Malin (1924-1994) graduated in 1954 from the State Art Institute in Tallinn, after which he worked as an artist, teacher, and spokesperson and interpreter of art life and art education in his home town of Tartu. Ilmar Malin played a great role in the emergence of surrealism and non-figurative art in the 1960s.
Among other things, Ilmar Malin created several large-scale works, monumental paintings, made for Mooste, Tartu, Rapla and Rakvere, or multi-part painting series. "Meeste mängud" ["Men's Games"] is an eight-part painting series. There are significant differences between the final result and the sketch, and comparing them gives an idea of the artist's creative process.
acf6b91374119928ad4ac690df994b19c993c0fd:
Aleksander Mülberg studied painting at the art courses of the Estonian Art Society in 1913-1914 and in 1915-1916 at Ants Laikmaa's studio school. On 21 November 1917, Mülberg founded, together with other young artists Balder Tomasberg, Oskar Kallis and Aleksander Krims, the society Vikerla, whose aim was "to promote creative thought and carry within itself the 'sacred fire' of art".
Mülberg's 10-sheet album of linocuts "Primeurs", published in 1920 in Tartu by the publishing house Arlekiin, which supported modern art, shows the artist's search for the formal methods of modern art.
In 1921 the artist left for Paris, where he spent the last 10 years of his life.
67ebfbfa99b208dfafd1b31bc7d3ff090341d188:
A selection of works created between 1944 and 1960 by one of the classics of Estonian art, an early female artist Salome Trei (1905-1995), expands the overview of her lesser-known post-World War II creative period.
Salome Trei, born in Kuressaare, studied graphic art in Tallinn at the State School of Arts and Crafts from 1929 to 1934, and finished the 6-year course cum laude. She then studied at Pallas in Tartu, which she completed in the 1939 graduating class.
The artist emigrated from Estonia in 1944. Having stayed in DP camps in Germany, she later lived in the USA, where she worked mainly as an applied artist, creating textile and commercial graphic designs for various companies.
8cc31862230e20c078141583c587611419632e0c: six grotesque male figures: upper left, half-figure of a man with thinning hair, mouth open, a sausage knife in his left hand, wearing a suit. In the middle, a quarter-figure of a man, hand at his chest, little finger touching his nose, other fingers spread. On the right, a quarter-figure of a man with an upright tuft of hair, large teeth showing through his open mouth. Below, a half-figure of a man, a pipe in his half-open mouth. In the middle, an elongated head with an upright tuft of hair, gapped teeth, a hooked nose and a wide-open mouth. On the right, a half-figure of a man in a suit, sitting, a drop falling from the tip of his long sharp nose, his left hand resting on his cheek, his right hand in front of him, on a sheet of paper and a pen lying on the table
bb30fc8e4ba0076445dea7f8fdbddd21c25f76a7: Three-part card with four vignettes, on the front left a large number "5", along the top edge hang side by side five coats of arms with a u-shaped ground plan, depicting (from left to right): a pegasus, a bird's feather, a harp, two theatre masks and three triangular shapes, below on the right the inscription: "Ball", on the verso of the front side, on the right a leafy branch, towards which a bird is flying, the sun in the sky, on the middle section the invitation text in French, on the right section, within a grid, a roe deer in profile leaping to the right, on the outer side the invitation text in Estonian, on the middle section a still life with a sheet of paper, a theatre mask, a trumpet, a palette, part of a column with an Ionic capital, and drapery
509ac679da2341383d615697ea3d385bf2526c91:
Eduard Wiiralt's watercolour "Portrait of a Woman" belongs to his so-called Antrain series of 1929. In that year, while staying in Antrain, Brittany, in connection with a commission, the artist produced a number of drawings and watercolours whose range of expression extends from fantastic realism to extreme grotesquerie and tormenting visions.
The graphic artist used the original drawings and watercolours of the Antrain series a little later in creating his most famous compositions, "Hell" (etching, copper engraving, 1930-1932) and "Cabaret" (etching, copper engraving, 1931).
The original watercolour "Portrait of a Woman" complements this highly valuable series in the Art Museum of Estonia.
36b6c99c433c506290c97aabaa149c9497cc67fb: Geometric shapes and their mutual relationships have repeatedly interested artists of the modernist era. In his four-part series "Blue Skies", executed in coloured photo-print technique, Silver Vahtre examines the relationship between the sphere and the cube, arriving at the witty conclusion that combining them produces a cone. The juxtaposition of geometric shapes with symmetrical images of the sky refers to fractal theory, little known in late Soviet Estonia, according to which natural forms have a structure just as regular as artificial ones. The series was first exhibited at the artist's solo exhibition at Kiek in de Kök in 1983.
9968482dbc9e8720d3fdedc074294c2a136760c5: Paul Kuimet's work was created for the exhibition "Landscape Runs Through the House", curated by Eero Epner, Tõnis Saadoja and the artist himself, held in 2023 at the Tartu Art Museum. According to the artist himself, it is the most poetic exhibition he has ever taken part in. The question was raised of how it is possible to see landscape in the year 2023. It turned out that this is possible even outside the context of the climate crisis or the Anthropocene. The series of three analogue-technique images carries the calm emotion of the exhibition. All three works are enlarged from the same negative. The artist plays with exposure time and filter settings, which determine the final result.
0ea1a6f302bac67c673bd93d5966b978b15d55db:
The works and archive of Gunnar Neeme (1918-2005) arrived in Estonia from Australia with the support of the "Compatriots Programme" project. Along with his paintings, four works on paper also arrived at the Art Museum of Estonia. These are a fine addition to the collection of Estonian exile art.
Gunnar Neeme, who settled in Australia in 1949, was a well-known book illustrator (his interpretation of the epic "Kalevipoeg" is especially significant), painter, graphic artist, applied artist and sculptor. Neeme was also a member of the Melbourne artists' organisation Victorian Artists Society, and his art-critical and philosophical writings were published in its monthly journal.
0cbad23f4b8b568f41ad8fc28716a1526bc47702: In a city (in Tartu's urban space), against the background of ruins (upper left, the ruins of the Vanemuine Theatre), seven working men in the foreground. On the left, a man standing in profile facing right, a bar held vertically between his hands. On the right, two men side by side, hoisting a thick pipe upright towards the viewer. Behind them, on the left, two standing men side by side: the left one in profile facing right, a shovel on his right shoulder; the other frontal, his left hand pointing to the right, towards the centre, his gaze in the same direction. At the right edge, two men: one standing in full view, head in profile facing right; the other further back, standing frontally, a pickaxe between his hands, head in profile facing right
6fabd15819b544115f1c2b69c9481a75594be198:
Toomas Kalve is a lecturer at the Tartu Art College and an internationally known photographic artist who, since 1987, has been photographing onto various glass plates and films, using wooden plate cameras. He captures still lifes, landscapes, interiors, birds and models in black and white. Kalve tones the black-and-white contact prints brown.
In this case it is a series of images of his still lifes. To stage his still lifes he prefers to use old objects, or, as the artist himself has said, objects that have a certain stabilised energy of their own. The technique gives them the appearance characteristic of old photographs.
f9149be2966114f43e5a70e5448373b2c257b5f8: Eugeni Noormägi is among the lesser-known names of Estonian exile art. Having begun his art studies with Ants Laikmaa and at the Pallas Art School, Noormägi left Estonia for America as early as 1926, while still in his early twenties. Fate then took the female artist to Denmark, where, after continuing her art studies in Copenhagen and Paris, she developed into a recognised artist. Noormägi's modernist work with its subdued colouring is a good example of the Nordic line represented in Estonian exile art. It expands our knowledge of the women artists who began their art studies in Estonia at the beginning of the last century.
9ea9ecd2ce19945fc06ed7036ce2258a2673eb96:
Vello Vinna's works are a notable example of the creative output of the generation of Estonian graphic artists who emerged in the late 1960s and early 1970s, distinguished by a coherent and markedly personal visual system. Vinna's distinctive visual world is based on masterly command of graphic art as a technique, a refined treatment of imagery, and witty connections.
The forceful treatment of black-and-white surfaces in Vinna's etching "Flight" creates a series of expressive graphic images and signs. A bold surrealist collage merges Vinna's imaginative world with the iconography of the Cold War era and the attributes of (Western) pop culture.
8615b6af0b24c2017a991e1d55a694c2c90a3b82: Reti Saks (b. 1960) graduated from ERKI in 1987, and to this day works mainly as a graphic artist, being internationally active and having received several accolades. The artist also creates sculptures and book illustrations. Reti Saks's artistic message is conveyed by a single (or several) genderless figure(s) of childlike proportions in an empty black-and-white pictorial space. With minimalist means, the graphic artist conveys anguished, often cryptic states of mind. One direction in Saks's work is devoted to the emergence of the image, as is the pair "Portrays" (2014). Compared with the intaglio print sheet, the refined preliminary drawing has a more immediate effect.
bb004c51ee981e25cd2721c300fc1c20997352fa: The painter and etcher Gottlieb Christian Welté was born in 1747 in Wiesbaden (Biebrich), worked in Mainz and Frankfurt, came to Estonia to Põltsamaa Castle, and died at Lohu Manor in 1792. With his small-format genre paintings and etchings he well matched the taste of his era. This work, too, depicts an intimate scene with a pair of lovers in nature, characteristic of the period. The Art Museum of Estonia holds several paintings, one etching and one sepia drawing by Gottlieb Christian Welté, to which this drawing is a valuable addition. The work's value is further enhanced by its period-appropriate framing.
2e15265a3e3d8602a9de2ebdbbd343782c3bec10:
A) In the centre, a standing male nude turned 1/2 to the right, head facing forward, hand on hip, legs apart. Beside him on the right, a male nude kneeling on one knee, body bent forward, hand on the knee, head in profile facing right. Upper right, a man's head is indicated, crossed out with three lines.
B) On the left, a comic male figure turned to the right, pulling nails from a table, the man's phallus showing from his trousers, pincers shown separately. On the right, two standing working male figures, hammering a nail into a wall. On the man on the right, a knotted male member shows from his trousers. On the left, separately, a hammer held in a clenched fist. Below, two hands with a chisel.
ec620782515dbe747c75deee96db46f4042119a0:
The work "Jump Without Landing" by Concordia Klar, one of the most renowned Estonian female graphic artists, can be counted among the more important works of her early period. The mezzotint technique later became especially typical of Klar.
"Jump Without Landing" is graphically simple in composition, yet contains numerous allusions and symbols characteristic of the Soviet period, especially of 1970s art (a fool-chronicler, a parachute, gondola posts in Venetian canals, roses-joy, etc.) As additional information, it is also interesting that the engraving was exhibited in 1972 at the collateral exhibition of the XXXVI Venice Biennale.
fc1dc5c7cc1ab20abc82d84e03f678d74c47e604: Geometric shapes and their mutual relationships have interested artists of the modernist era again and again. Silver Vahtre's four-part series „Punased taevad“, executed in the technique of coloured photo print, is dedicated to the more beloved geometric shape of modern art, the square. The juxtaposition of the geometric shape with symmetrical images of the sky refers to fractal theory, little known in late Soviet Estonia, according to which natural forms have a structure just as regular as artificial ones. The series was first exhibited at the artist's solo exhibition in 1983 at Kiek-in-de-Kök.
7430e810f38b54b355f6a1c7ee0e1c8be493102c:
The study-period works from the 1930s by one of the classics of Estonian art, an early female artist Salome Trei (1905-1995), broaden the overview of the Art Museum of Estonia's collections regarding the artist's pre-World War II creative period.
Born in Kuressaare, Salome Trei studied graphic art in Tallinn at the State School of Applied Art from 1929-1934 and completed the school's 6-year course cum laude. Trei then studied at Pallas in Tartu and graduated with the class of 1939.
Salome Trei emigrated from Estonia in 1944, stayed in DP camps in Germany, and in her later period lived in the USA, where she worked mainly as an applied artist.
61c65767f4778db2d5d88ded3223cb72e031eba5: The late 1980s and early 1990s are associated in Estonian graphic art with an expressive manner of depiction, which marked a liberation from previous imagery and did not confine itself to the usual dimensions of graphic works either. Alongside conceptual geometricized graphic art, characteristic of the postmodernist spirit of the time, emerged forceful figurative treatments that addressed archaic forms and symbols. The work „Märjad juuksed“ represents both Urmas Viik's (b. 1961) large-format colour compositions of the 1980s-1990s and the graphic art of this period in the collection of the Art Museum of Estonia.
16065c01dcdf4d9ef35feac106461c80eaa7ad5a: In an interior, eight men in rich-folded, floor-length garments stand and converse. In the foreground on the left, a bare-headed, bearded man in profile facing right, left hand at the right shoulder, right arm bent at the elbow in front. On the right, a man with a turban on his head, beard and moustache, in profile facing left, hands crossed below. In the centre, a younger man with smooth, longer hair and a short beard, facing forward, right hand vertically in front of the chest, left arm bent at the elbow at waist level. On the left, an older man in profile facing right, behind whom the heads of four men are visible, all with beards, three with turbans on their heads.
826c84c62f898f1a7ddd88b6ca3d3f6207dc65c6: In „Homo EKAdemicus“ Linnap ironically addresses, through images enlarged from the Estonian Art and Architecture Biographical Lexicon, the surprising continuation of Soviet-style manners of photo retouching in the present (!) era. It points to the differing pace at which chronological time and changes in mentality progress. The situation is paradoxical – the cold manner of portrait retouching from the repressive era turns otherwise mild-lyrical artists and art historians in the images de facto into outright Stalinist robots. The audience of the British Arnolfini gallery considered those portrayed to be, for example, representatives of dead generations.
0fc572215e5cec50f006e2224fb2e987851bfb66: Evi Tihemets (b. 1932) is one of the leading Estonian graphic artists. She has created works in a great variety of techniques and styles and has received numerous awards. These drawings are early works, in which we see the artist's personality forming. At the same time, these travel drawings characterize the era, the atmosphere of becoming freer and more liberal. After graduating from the art institute in 1958, Evi Tihemets, like young artists of that time in general, did not have the opportunity to further her education in the world's art centres; this was replaced by journeys to various places in the Soviet Union.
aabaeb8f7ff0596bea267ddbd810b84a211b72b4:
Carl August Senff's (1770-1838) drawing depicts an unknown young man, but is marked by the author: Senff fec 1804 zu Dorpat (translation: Senff made this in 1804 in Tartu). The pencil and coloured-pencil drawing is worked through in a filigree and lively manner. There is no doubt that this profile portrait is an original work by Senff. Although the model is not known, he probably belongs to the circle of the reopened University of Tartu, though he could also be some other Livonian. 
Very few of Carl August Senff's portrait drawings have survived, and this work is further enhanced by its original frame and glass.
32048e91c8e4fc030730d17b73a468c1e74d159c:
Painted in oil on canvas, depicting against a background a blue sky, grain stacks, a truck and a threshing machine with working human figures, on the right a horse with a cart and the front part of a tractor, beside which stands a male figure, on the left a truck seen from behind, beside which stand two male figures, in the foreground two female and two male figures, one of whom has a bicycle, and grain sacks.
The canvas is fastened with nails to a frame, in the corners of which triangular wooden pieces are nailed down; the outer frame is painted white, on the reverse at the top edge there is text and a year. The painting is unsigned.
f86a210a27185c3923e649b7c7de1d156adb6fa3: Reti Saks (b. 1960) graduated from ERKI in 1987; she still works today mainly as a graphic artist, being internationally active and having received numerous accolades. The artist also creates sculptures and book illustrations. Reti Saks's artistic message is conveyed by a single (or several) genderless figure(s) of childlike proportions in an empty black-and-white pictorial space. Using minimalist means, the graphic artist conveys anguished, often cryptic states of mind. The pair „Segadus segaduses“ (2009) shows the original drawing and the print engraving as stages of the graphic artist's working process and different art media.
981bce24a1c327bd64a7059d60c5e10eb9fa80cb: The work consists of a whole row of heads modelled in clay, the impulse for whose creation the artist received from the sculptures of St. John's Church in Tartu. Edith Karlson creates her gallery of portraits with the help of acquaintances. They all worked in the artist's studio, most of them having never touched clay before. The artist had the ambition to ask that she herself be portrayed. Yet each author puts a great part of themselves into their work, thereby also creating their own presence in the gallery of portraits. The artist exhibits the portraits in such a way that they attain a significance as timeless as the works of St. John's Church.
e151c4dbf357e594b4eda1f3a3a429f82d8e3741: Salome Trei's (1905-1995) drawings, made after the Second World War in refugee camps in Germany, are rare documents of that era. Trei, who came from Kuressaare, studied graphic art in Tallinn at the State School of Applied Art from 1929-1934 and completed the school's 6-year course cum laude. Trei then studied at Pallas in Tartu, which she completed in 1939. No print was added to her high-period graphic art after 1944. The artist emigrated from Estonia in 1944 and in her later period lived in the USA, where she worked mainly as an applied artist, creating designs for textiles and applied graphic art.
ac2c3a00deda39e1aed1ca289a1c8e8406ddd581:
A story based on documentary narratives about people who were forced to leave Estonia as refugees 70 years ago, and about those people who have only recently arrived in Estonia as refugees. Estonians who have lived long lives in exile share memories of the hospitality of the country that received them. At Estonia's only reception centre for asylum seekers, located 1.8 km from the Russian border near an abandoned village, people who have been awaiting an asylum decision for many months tell of their experiences.

The work was filmed in 2013 in Stockholm and in Estonia near the village of Jaama in Illuka Parish.
c0017611bea2004806ec008141663dcc203a47dc: A composition built on three vertical axes from fantastical heads filling the whole sheet: in the centre of the sheet a machine-man firing from a cannon-like nose, whose armoured hand reaches down to the right, from a screaming head on the right coins are flying out, above which is a fortress-like crown, on the left a stem of heads growing out of a skull, on which are branches with cat-faces and birds; among the described heads there is also, for example, a woman's face crowned with a cat-head (lower left), a trumpeter (upper centre), a grinning man whose necktie is a female nude (lower right).
bee05ab2a465a441ede135c12c65847f344434f8:
In a rectangle, two men, in front an older man with dark curly hair, behind a younger man with a moustache, sword in his right hand, in the distance a man holding his head fleeing, and a man with moustache and beard.
Below the rectangle, the author's text in ink:
Jüri Kuuskemaa, the guardian of Old Tallinn's virginity, chased away architects driven by the desire to build, with a fiery sword.
Leo Gens, who takes a tolerant view of the loss of innocence, tries to admonish him.
Heinz Valk hurries to reconcile the brawlers, being of the opinion that the maiden has already been embraced by too many lovers for it to be worth fighting over her innocence any longer.
be81c0ede3ba88fdb0e7732672e4d8fe58d19f04: On an oval background consisting of bubble-like stones, some of which are cone-shaped, 16 capsule-like objects (stylized heads) and a rhombus. Inside the rhombus, larger, smaller and tiny circles repeat, in which are multi-headed dragons, snakes, horses' legs, among them figures of women with hats on horseback (a motif common in Aksinin's works). The woman's hands are mostly down and the pose is static; in one instance she plays a pipe, and in another a snake flies out of her mouth. In the lower corner of the rhombus is the text „Июнь VI“, on the left, on top of two „capsule-heads“, the numbers „11“ and „153“.
50a3eedd70ae24d9d7488976a0f3c380a382e01a:
In an oriental room (on a terrace), a woman lies on a carpet, a man's head between her hands on her lap. On the right stand a woman and a man, on the left the figure of a man (a warrior). In the centre a sphinx and in the background a sailboat.

The story of Salome (Salomé), a young, beautiful woman (femme fatale), has been interpreted very often in art. In the biblical text, Salome was the daughter of Herodias, who with her veil dance enticed her stepfather Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee and Palestine. As a reward she desired the head of John the Baptist, at her mother's instigation, because John the Baptist had condemned their marriage. Salome brought the head on a platter to her mother.
b83192e32aeb969b19d04acb825a66ab1e10b9e2: Kalli Kalde's print series „Kirjad Gulagist“ is an interesting example of the artist's engagement with her family history and archive, creating a creative interpretation based on it. The series is based on letters and photographs from her grandfather's period in the Vorkuta forced labour camp, the images of which were synthesised into multi-layered compositions using offset lithography technique. To the documentary layers is added an emotional dimension through images embroidered in red, by means of which the artist has visualised the experiences of both those imprisoned and the family members left behind.
4e7a0b12ea8d977bcdfd4dc80b8fc90d983ddc17: Evi Tihemets is one of the leading Estonian graphic artists. She has created works in very different techniques and styles and has received numerous awards. This drawing is an early work, in which we see the artist's personality taking shape. At the same time, this travel drawing characterises the era, the atmosphere of becoming freer and more liberal. After graduating from the art university in 1958, Evi Tihemets, like young artists of that time in general, did not have the opportunity to further her education in the world's art centres, which was replaced by travels to various places in the Soviet Union.
8edc2eb8a1c9678323a38dd62d4cb1fab9788cfd: Kaljo Põllu's interest in the history and myths of kindred peoples led, among other things, to expeditions organised with art students. Parallel to the research work, there was also a creative interpretation of the material: thus the monumental print series „Kalivägi“ (1978–1984) engages with Finno-Ugric ethnographic and mythological heritage in the form of artistic interpretation. The unique series, which grew into a 65-sheet monumental narrative, is not represented in full in the collections of the Art Museum of Estonia, which is why it is important to assemble as complete a set as possible.

Among these are also the sheets „Produktsioon“ and „Multiplikatsioon“ executed in offset print, which complement well the works created in the suprematist spirit in the print collection of the Art Museum of Estonia, also representing a series hitherto missing here.

a4fd74a159178991ae1575eeec3e38ef964ef964: Helgi Hirv's „Tartu motiiv“ is quite notable in the context of its time: unlike the landscape treatments favoured in the official art of Soviet Estonia in the 1950s, which focused on the building of the socialist state and society, this work presents a view of the town of Tartu with a subjective and poetic viewpoint, in which the signs of the Soviet era are rather suppressed. Developing the intaglio print technique, which was disapproved of in Soviet art conception, this sheet complements well the lyrical view-graphics by Helgi Hirv in this technique held in the Art Museum of Estonia.
a5c007cc5f7ce1b9d352510935e88282e08989db: The Dance of Death motif, widespread in the Middle Ages, was actualised again in the modernism of the early 20th century, depicting the eternal cycle of human life. The motif of the dance of death or life also appears in the work of several other Estonian artists of this period, uniting both existential and artistic searches. In Mart Pärt's interpretation of the Dance of Death, who studied under Nikolai Triik at the Tallinn School of Applied Art, the influences of his teacher are perceptible, reflected, among other things, in the (late) Art Nouveau stylisation of the work and its expressionist and national-romantic treatment.

7f83172aee10c6e243fa218640f681f2b4e5fbfe: Prints from the series "Flowers" – The minimalist prints capture the first two layers of the sheets from the series "Flowers", executed in the complex and distinctive silk-screen printing technique developed by Malle Leis and Villu Jõgeva. The tondo-format silk-screen series was commissioned in the 1970s for decorating the interior of Rydzyna Castle (Poland), which had been reconstructed as a residence for engineers. In addition to their cultural-historical value, these prints reveal Malle Leis's ability to create a strong image that works as a whole even in the case of an unfinished depiction.

fbdf03fb2ee3557e78f1a906f1ca67a3da6bce38: Muravskaja, who usually reacts sharply to social problems, turns this time to poetic abstract imagery seen through water and light. She has said of her works: "With my works I also invite the viewer to slow down and re-tune their gaze – to step aside from the endless stream of news and images, in order to restore sensitivity to light and time, and to notice how the image is born here and now. It is a journey to the border between the visible and the invisible, which brings the viewer back to a heightened physical presence."
8a436076aa2cd0c50a82b3873ae161ce904931bd: Benjamin Vasserman's (b. 1949) work "Avarus I" is an excellent example of the recent creative work of the well-known Estonian printmaker. Vasserman began in the 1980s with colour intaglio printing (etching, aquatint) and has moved towards large formats and complex digital technique. In his works spatiality is combined with geometrism. In the series "Avarus" ("Space", begun in 2014) the artist deals with problems such as the intensity of colour, science-fiction space, the meeting of the cosmos and the microworld, a multiplicity of variations and visions in the subconscious.
2067a5e8234e6cb2942478adf60f2994557ade6f: Maria Kapajeva has taken up a theme that is not exactly the newest but remains stubbornly topical – the place and role of women in society and their right to decide the goals of their own body and life. The theme received a comprehensive artistic expression at the solo exhibition "When the World Blows Up, I Hope to Leave Dancing" held at the Tallinn Art Hall gallery in 1920. The exhibition attracted lively attention, and its impact was amplified by the background of events taking place in Poland that same year, where thousands of women came out against the banning of abortion.

The exhibition was titled "A Hundred Dreams in the Middle of the Sea"

f40e462ca93fd6129e0ea561f53108e416672cf3: The beginning of Ly Lestberg's independent creative work fell at the end of the 1980s, when neo-expressionism and personal mythology dominated the work of young artists. Lestberg's dynamic, upward-striving figures in glowing tones are not only among the most characteristic but also among the best works of the young art of that period, and certainly the best in Lestberg's own work of that time. Lestberg has only a few works of this kind, since she quite quickly moved on to photography. This is a very necessary addition to the Art Museum of Estonia's collection of 1980s art.
12160889c366a3c13353abd3ab61b011483ceac4: The series "Pictures from an Exhibition" dates from Tõnu Noorits's earlier creative period. The series has also been called a flirtation with painting. Here the central place is occupied by the pictorial world of Ilmar Kruusamäe and Oleg Bogdanov, to which the legendary Matti Milius and a female nude have been added. Through black-and-white photography he shapes from this jumble his own simplified, yet at the same time expressive, pictorial world. The photographs are executed with the utmost precision and accuracy, and finally coloured by the photographic artist with colours from a palette completely different from the original.
b31ec979e0218b7228c2466dd8ddd8d4ce3ce792: "Rahutus" ("Unrest") is one of Eduard Wiiralt's last major works and can be considered his swan song, which Wiiralt began to plan already in 1949 and on which he worked in the years 1950-1952. "Rahutus" is executed in a mixed technique (also called a synthetic technique), which had been characteristic of Wiiralt's work already from 1949 and was based mainly on soft-ground etching. Given the canonical nature of the work, it is important for the Art Museum of Estonia to preserve various states of the sheet and the first prints from the edition.
703d257aa74215b169d45219e786b90cfb29bbc4: Reti Saks (b. 1960) graduated from ERKI in 1987, and to this day she works mainly as a printmaker, being internationally active and having received several accolades. The artist also creates sculptures and book illustrations. Reti Saks's artistic message is conveyed by a single (or several) genderless figure(s) with childlike proportions in an empty black-and-white pictorial space. With minimalist means the printmaker conveys anguished, often cryptic states of mind. One direction in Saks's work is devoted to the emergence of the image, and such is also the pair "Portreteerib" (2014).

In the pictures the artist depicts herself as a cloth doll.

8eaf66ad5d9d97b6603444b51e36253153ab795e:
Evi Tihemets (b. 1932) is one of the best-known and most prolific Estonian printmakers. In her versatile body of work she has occasionally turned to large-scale graphic forms, and such is also the collage "Päikesevarjutus" ["Solar Eclipse"], exhibited at the artist's anniversary exhibition in the summer of 2017.
The artist has combined fragments of her own printed impressions, different papers, and thus created a grandiose abstract composition, which she has dedicated to a special natural phenomenon that occurred in the summer of 1990, a total solar eclipse.
e17f52ac53c9ab86e7da7b6e618ef3681426cbad: The caricatures of book illustrator and caricaturist Elle Tikerpää complement well the collection representing the field in question in the graphic art collection of the Art Museum of Estonia. As a conceptual continuation of the tradition of satirical images formed in the early years of the Republic of Estonia (Gori, Otto Krusten and others), they dissect (e.g. alongside Heinz Valk's caricatures) the topical social problems of their era - moving on to the context of the Soviet period and the time of Estonia's regained independence, where a separate place is given to caricatures on art-related themes.
3cf74f666f09b4fd7418b1772462548f5569a094: Viktor Timofejev's drawing, thanks to the author's Latvian background, is expanding the small Baltic sub-collection of the graphic art collection of the Art Museum of Estonia. The work of this internationally recognised artist is a vivid example of the skilful use of traditional drawing technique in creating contemporary, ambiguously open images, generating a new type of abstraction through the estrangement of everyday views surrounding the author (in this case the starting point has been a view of the artist's bathroom window and its reflection on the wall)
